unit.title: Si Clauses (Real Conditions)
unit.subtitle: Talking about real, likely situations with 'if'

grammar.title: If this happens, that follows: the first conditional
grammar.intro: When a condition is real and likely — something that genuinely might happen — Spanish uses si + the present indicative. The result can be in the present, the future, or a command. The golden rule: after si for a real condition, never use the future. Say Si tengo tiempo, never si tendré tiempo.

sections.heading: si + present, then present / future / imperative
sections.body: The si clause states the condition in the present indicative. The result clause is flexible — pick the mood that fits your meaning:

ex.en: If I have time, I go to the cinema.
If I have time, I'll go to the cinema.

sections.heading: Never 'si + future'
sections.body: This is the mistake to avoid. Even when the result is clearly in the future, the si clause itself stays in the present. English lets you say “if I will have time”; Spanish does not:

ex.en: If you study, you'll pass the exam.

ex.es: Si llueve mañana, nos quedamos en casa.
ex.en: If it rains tomorrow, we'll stay home.

sections.heading: Either order works
sections.body: You can lead with the si clause or the result. When si comes first, separate the two halves with a comma; when it comes second, no comma is needed:

ex.en: If it rains, don't go out.
Don't go out if it rains.

takeaways: Result can be present, future, or imperative: voy / iré / no salgas.
Never use the future after si: Si tengo (not 'si tendré').
Si-clause first → comma; result first → no comma.

mistakes.w: Si tendré tiempo, iré al cine.
mistakes.r: Si tengo tiempo, iré al cine.
mistakes.why: After si for a real condition, use the present, never the future.
The si clause stays in the present even when the result is future.
When the si clause comes first, add a comma before the result.

exercises.prompt_en: If I have time, I'll go to the cinema.
exercises.ok: ¡Correcto! Después de si, presente: si tengo.
exercises.no: After si for a real condition, use the present: “si tengo”, never the future.

exercises.prompt_en: If you study, you'll pass the exam.
exercises.ok: ¡Exacto! si + presente, resultado en futuro: aprobarás.
exercises.no: The result here is a future consequence: “aprobarás”.

exercises.prompt: Build: “If it rains, don't go out.”
exercises.no: “Si llueve, no salgas” — present after si, then a command.

exercises.prompt: Si ___ tiempo, voy al parque. (tener, yo)
exercises.prompt_en: If I have time, I go to the park.
exercises.hint: Present indicative of tener, yo form. Never the future.
exercises.ok: ¡Bien! Si tengo tiempo — presente, no futuro.
exercises.no: Use the present after si: “si tengo”, not 'si tendré'.

exercises.prompt: Match each si-condition to its natural result.
exercises.ok: ¡Excelente! You've matched real conditions to their results.

exercises.no: It was: “Si llueve, no salgas.” (If it rains, don't go out.)
